Centrifugation. A laboratory technique that uses centrifugal force to separate particles of different densities from a liquid mixture. By spinning samples at high speeds, the denser components migrate outward to the bottom of the container, forming a compact pellet, while the less dense liquid layer, called the supernatant, can be easily decanted or pipetted off.

The behavior of particles during centrifugation is governed by the Svedberg equation, which relates the sedimentation velocity of a particle to its molecular mass, density, and frictional coefficient, defining the sedimentation coefficient expressed in Svedberg units. Ultracentrifugation, a technique pioneered by Theodor Svedberg, spins samples at extremely high speeds, often exceeding one hundred thousand revolutions per minute, to separate proteins and other macromolecules.

Centrifugation has many specialized applications. Density gradient centrifugation uses cesium chloride or sucrose gradients to separate cellular components or macromolecules based on their buoyant density. This method was the key technique in the famous Meselson-Stahl experiment in nineteen fifty-eight, which used cesium chloride density gradients to prove the semi-conservative replication of DNA, separating DNA labeled with heavy nitrogen-fifteen from light nitrogen-fourteen.

In medical diagnostics, centrifugation separates whole blood into plasma, a buffy coat of white blood cells and platelets, and a pellet of dense red blood cells. This peer separation technique relies on density differences under rotational force, whereas industrial gas centrifuges spin gaseous uranium hexafluoride to separate fissile uranium-235 from uranium-238 based on mass.
